Thus did Raghava advance, amidst the eulogies of his friends 
the focus of every eye and heart, sen:ne and imperturbable. 
Those who were unable to behold him or were unnoticed by 
him, became objects of contempt to others, nay, they were a 
reproach to themselves. The all-compassionate Ramachandra 
looked on each of the four castes with equal condescension. 
Each loved him according to his capacity. 
Passing the temples, the sacred groves and pavilions, Shri 
Ramachandra circumambulated them in reverence. He now 
beheld the royal palace, resembling a white cloud, its towers 
like the snow-capped peaks of Mount Kailasa, its balconies 
seeming almost to reach the skies like the fire chariots of the 
gods ; the pleasure houses set with precious gems, caused the 
whole palace to excel all those on earth and rival even the abode 
oflndra. 
Approaching his father's palace, Sbri Rams passed through 
the three gateways guarded by archers, and proceeded on foot 
through the fourth and fifth enclosures. There, leaving his 
attendants, he entered the private apartments of the king. 
The multitude seeing Rams enter the palace were filled with 
joy and awaited his coming forth as the sea awaits the coming 
of the full moon.

It is rare indeed for a man to be consistently happy. Has his

brief.summary_1line: Rama visits Dasharatha, sees his distress, and Kaikeyi reveals her demand: Bharata’s coronation and Rama’s fourteen‑year exile to honor the king’s old promise.

image_candidates.scene_text: Rama bows at the feet of the pale, grief‑stricken King Dasharatha who sits speechless beside the stern Kaikeyi on the royal couch.
Kaikeyi coldly declares Rama’s exile while the devastated king weeps silently, unable to look at his son.
Calm and resolute, Rama vows to obey his father even if it means fire, poison, or the sea, standing before the trembling king.

deep.rich_summary: Rama arrives at the royal palace amid the joy and admiration of Ayodhya’s people, moving serenely through the sacred spaces and into the king’s private chambers. There he finds King Dasaratha pale, anguished, and unable to speak, seated beside Queen Kaikeyi. Disturbed by his father’s condition, Rama humbly asks the cause and declares his absolute obedience to his father’s will, even to the point of death. Kaikeyi, cold and calculating, reveals the truth: long ago the king granted her two boons, and she now claims them—Bharata must be crowned king and Rama must go into exile in the Dandaka forest for fourteen years. Rama receives the decree without visible distress, while Dasaratha, foreseeing his son’s suffering, is crushed by grief. The moment marks the decisive turning point that sends Rama into exile and sets the epic’s central journey in motion.

highlight_spans.why: Introduces Rama’s revered presence among the people and the anticipation surrounding his expected coronation.
Dasaratha’s silent anguish and Rama’s alarm create the emotional tension that precedes the revelation.
Rama’s vow of absolute obedience—willing even to die if commanded—reveals his defining virtue of filial devotion.
Kaikeyi finally states her demands: Bharata’s coronation and Rama’s fourteen‑year exile, the pivotal command that drives the rest of the epic.

top_scenes.scene_text: Rama entering the dim royal chamber, bowing at the feet of a pale, tearful King Dasaratha while the stern Kaikeyi sits beside him on the couch.
Kaikeyi coldly declaring her boons—Bharata crowned and Rama exiled—while the king collapses in grief and Rama stands calm and resolute.
